title: A Will for the Verdict
premise: Ada Fairweather, coroner of the coastal town of Marrow Bay, receives two letters the same morning: one confessing to a death she ruled accidental years ago, and one, unsigned, promising a fourth body before the trial. As she reopens her old files, she realizes the confessor knows details only someone inside the investigation could possess — and that the promised victim is the trial's star witness. Racing the calendar toward the hearing, Ada lays a trap using falsified case documents, forcing the killer to reveal themselves in the courthouse archive on the eve of testimony. The confession letter turns out to be written by the killer's dying twin, and Ada must choose between exposing a truth that will destroy an innocent family or letting a murderer walk free.
about_author: Elodie Voss is a former rural court reporter who spent a decade transcribing small-town trials across the Pacific Northwest before turning to fiction. She writes mysteries from a converted boathouse, where she keeps a wall of unsolved cases as research and reminder.

chapters.title: Two Envelopes, One Morning
chapters.summary: Ada Fairweather opens her mail at the coroner's office and finds a handwritten confession to the 2019 drowning of Daniel Pryce — a death she ruled accidental — followed by a second, typed letter promising 'one more before the gavel falls.' Her POV establishes her meticulous mind and quiet pride in her three unofficial solves. The emotional beat is unease: someone has been watching her work for years.

chapters.title: The Grave That Doesn't Fit
chapters.summary: In Ada's POV, she exhumes her notes on Pryce and finds a discrepancy she missed: the tide tables contradict the water in his lungs. Meanwhile Deputy Ray Okafor, her reluctant ally from a past case, warns her the district attorney wants no pre-trial complications. The beat is mounting dread as Ada realizes her own signature sits atop a lie someone else engineered.

chapters.title: The Witness Who Counts Backward
chapters.summary: Shifting to the POV of Maren Kettle, the trial's key witness and a retired court clerk, we see her receiving anonymous phone calls reciting her own testimony back to her. She dismisses them until she notices her front gate open and footprints matching her late husband's boots. The beat is isolation — the killer is rehearsing her fear like lines in a play.

chapters.title: What the Archive Keeps
chapters.summary: Ada breaks into the county records annex after hours and discovers pages of the Pryce file photocopied and returned slightly wrong — reordered, annotated in pencil. Only three people had access: Okafor, the DA, and the late file clerk, Ruth Ambrose. The beat is betrayal-tinged suspicion as Ada realizes the killer isn't hiding the truth; they're curating it.

chapters.title: A Handwriting Like Home
chapters.summary: Ada recognizes the confession's handwriting as belonging to Elias Ambrose, Ruth's son, now terminally ill in a care facility — but Elias was twelve when Pryce died. In his POV, we learn he copied the letter from something his mother left him, believing it his duty to send. The beat is grief: a dying man trying to settle his mother's debts with borrowed words.

chapters.title: The Fourth Body, Promised
chapters.summary: Maren disappears the night before her deposition. Ada's POV races through the town's fog-bound streets while Okafor stalls the DA with a fabricated lead. They find Maren unharmed but drugged, staged beside a copy of the Pryce autopsy — a message meant for Ada alone. The beat is fury hardening into resolve: the killer wants an audience, not just a victim.

chapters.title: Paper Traps
chapters.summary: Ada plants doctored documents in the courthouse archive — each version containing a different false detail about the Pryce timeline — knowing the killer reads everything before investigators do. Told partly through the DA's anxious POV, the chapter builds the trap while he suspects Ada herself. The beat is chess-like tension: every file drawer is now a loaded spring.

chapters.title: The Version That Vanishes
chapters.summary: One doctored file disappears overnight — the one naming Ruth Ambrose as the original forger of the tide report. Ada's POV confirms the killer is protecting Ruth's memory, narrowing the suspect pool to those who loved her. A confrontation with Okafor nearly breaks their alliance when he accuses her of manufacturing evidence. The beat is loneliness at the center of the hunt.

chapters.title: Gavel Eve
chapters.summary: The night before trial, Ada stakes out the annex and catches the killer: Ruth's other child, Nora Ambrose, a paralegal on the defense team, who altered the file years ago to shield her mother and killed Pryce accidentally during a panicked confrontation. Nora holds a scalpel to the final document, ready to burn the last proof. The beat is terrible clarity — loyalty and crime braided together.

chapters.title: A Will for the Verdict
chapters.summary: In the climactic standoff, Ada talks Nora down by reading aloud Ruth's real will, which named both children equally — proof that love didn't require the lie. Nora surrenders; Elias dies peacefully days later, believing the debt paid. The trial proceeds with clean evidence, and Ada signs a corrected autopsy report, finally ruling Pryce's death what it truly was. The beat is bittersweet restoration: truth served, at cost.
